title: Design a Media Upload and Transcoding Pipeline
followUps: A creator uploads a 1.5 GB video from a phone on a train. The connection drops three times. Walk through the API calls the app makes and what the server stores after each drop.

A transcoding worker crashes 80% of the way through the 1080p rendition. What happens next, how does the system notice, and how do you avoid publishing a half-finished video or doing all the work twice?
A popular brand posts a video and 2 million viewers open it within 10 minutes. Trace a viewer's playback request and explain why your origin storage doesn't melt.
Processing compute is now the largest line on the cloud bill. Where would you look to cut it, and what does each option cost in quality or latency?
The same 300 MB promo video is uploaded 5,000 times by different franchise accounts of one brand. How would you notice and avoid storing and transcoding it 5,000 times, and what are the risks?

interviewer.approach: Strong answers keep large bytes off the application servers, model processing as an idempotent multi-step workflow, and use adaptive streaming behind a CDN for delivery. Requirements: uploads up to 2 GB / 20 minutes, resumable; validate format, duration and content policy; output HLS (or DASH) ladder (e.g. 240p-1080p) plus thumbnails and a preview; uploader sees progress and gets notified when ready or failed; publish only when all required renditions exist; playback starts fast on mobile. Estimates: 500k uploads/day ~6/s average, ~20/s peak; average 150 MB is 75 TB/day of uploads (~7 Gbps average); a 3-minute video at ~5 renditions takes ~1-2 CPU-minutes per rendition with a fast preset, so ~500k x 5 x 1.5 = ~3.75M CPU-minutes/day (~2,600 vCPUs continuous, more at peak); outputs roughly equal to input size (~75 TB/day), originals kept at a cheaper storage tier. Upload: client asks the API to create a video record (idempotency key), receives an upload id and presigned URLs for multipart/chunked upload directly to object storage (S3 multipart or a tus-style resumable protocol); on drop it asks which parts exist and resumes; on completion the client (or a storage event) marks the upload complete. Processing: storage event -> workflow orchestrator (Step Functions, Temporal, or a job table plus queues) that runs validate/probe, content checks, split into segments (GOP-aligned chunks) for parallel transcoding of each rendition, stitch/package into HLS, generate thumbnails, then publish; each task is idempotent (deterministic output paths keyed by video id + rendition + chunk, so a retried task overwrites rather than duplicates), with visibility timeouts/heartbeats so a crashed worker's task is retried, bounded retries and a dead-letter queue. Video state machine: CREATED -> UPLOADING -> UPLOADED -> PROCESSING -> READY/FAILED with per-rendition status; publish is an atomic state flip after all required renditions exist. Workers: autoscaled on queue depth, spot/preemptible instances (chunks make preemption cheap), GPU or hardware encoders where cost-effective; prioritise short videos and paying customers. Delivery: HLS manifests and segments served from a CDN with long cache TTLs (segments immutable), origin shield in front of object storage, signed URLs or tokens for private videos; mobile clients choose bitrate adaptively. Notifications: status changes published to an event bus -> push notifications and a status endpoint/WebSocket for the uploader. Cost: content hash of the original to deduplicate identical uploads (with care for privacy and takedowns), skip renditions above the source resolution, per-title encoding, lifecycle policies to move originals to cold storage, delete abandoned multipart uploads.
hints: Should a 2 GB file pass through your API servers? Who else could receive the bytes?
If the upload breaks at 60%, what does the client need to know to continue, and where is that state kept?
Transcoding a 20-minute video into five renditions takes a while. How could you make it finish faster and survive a worker crash?
What exactly does a phone download when a viewer presses play, and from where?
Which states can a video be in, and which component is allowed to move it to 'ready'?
pitfalls: Streaming uploads through the application servers, which ties up connections and bandwidth.
Single-request uploads with no resume, so mobile users restart large uploads from zero.
One worker transcoding a whole video into every rendition sequentially, so a crash loses all the work and long videos are slow.
Non-idempotent tasks (random output names, append-only writes), so retries create duplicate or partial outputs.
Publishing a video before all required renditions are complete, or with no state machine to say what is ready.
Serving progressive MP4 files from origin storage instead of adaptive streaming through a CDN.
No plan for compute and storage costs: keeping every original in hot storage, transcoding renditions above the source resolution, never cleaning up abandoned uploads.
facts: About 500,000 uploads per day, peaking at about 3 times the average rate in the evening.
Videos are up to 2 GB and 20 minutes; the average upload is about 150 MB and 3 minutes. About 70% of uploads come from phones, often over cellular networks.
Outputs: HLS with 5 renditions from 240p to 1080p (never above the source resolution), 3 thumbnails, and a 6-second silent preview clip.
Target: a 3-minute video is playable within 2 minutes of the upload finishing at p95; videos up to 20 minutes within 10 minutes.
Uploads must be checked for supported formats, corrupt files and a content-policy classifier (an existing internal service taking about 5 seconds per video) before publishing.
Uploaders see upload and processing progress in the app and get a push notification when the video is ready or has failed.
Viewers watch in the iOS and Android apps worldwide; a popular brand's video can get millions of views in its first hour. Some videos are private to a brand's team.
Originals must be kept for 1 year in case the platform re-encodes with new formats.
Compute and storage costs matter; the company already uses a major cloud provider's object storage, queues and CDN.
deepDives: Resumable uploads directly to object storage with presigned multipart URLs
The processing workflow: state machine, chunked parallel transcoding, idempotent tasks and crash recovery
Adaptive streaming delivery through a CDN, and private videos
Scaling and cost: autoscaling on queue depth, spot instances, prioritisation, deduplication and storage tiers
Progress tracking and notifications to the uploader
